opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a genuinely strange transition, and I think the honest answer is that it's both more exhilarating and more disorienting than I expected.

For most of my career, the craft of writing code was the thing that grounded me. There's a flow state you get into when you're holding a whole system in your head and translating it line by line. That feedback loop of typing, running, seeing it break, fixing it was very tactile. When you move to orchestrating agents, a lot of that tactile feeling goes away. You're no longer the person laying bricks; you're closer to the architect walking the site, checking whether the walls are where you thought they'd be.

What surprised me most is that the bottleneck moved. It used to be "how fast can I implement this?" Now it's "how clearly can I specify what I actually want?" and "how quickly can I verify that what came back is right?" Those turn out to be very different skills. A vague idea that I could have muddled through by hand, discovering what I wanted as I went, now produces a confident, plausible, slightly wrong result from an agent. So I've had to get much more disciplined about thinking up front: writing down intent, constraints, edge cases, what "done" means.

The other big shift is around trust and review. Early on I either over-trusted, accepting big diffs because they looked reasonable, or under-trusted and re-read every line, which killed the leverage. The middle ground I've landed on is investing heavily in verification infrastructure: good tests, type checks, small reviewable chunks, and asking the agent to explain its reasoning or flag what it's unsure about. The agent's work is only as valuable as my ability to confirm it's correct.

Then there's the parallelism, which is the part that feels genuinely new. I can have several agents working on different threads at once: one exploring a refactor, one writing tests, one investigating a bug. My job becomes managing attention and context switching, almost like an engineering manager with a very fast, very literal team. That's powerful, but it's also tiring in a different way. Instead of deep focus on one problem, it's lots of shallow check-ins, and I have to be careful not to lose the thread of the overall design.

And emotionally, I'll admit there's a bit of grief in it. Some of the joy of programming was the puzzle-solving itself. But I've found the joy relocates. It moves up a level, to system design, to product thinking, to the satisfaction of seeing something ambitious come together in days instead of months. I think the people who'll thrive are the ones who can let go of identifying with keystrokes and start identifying with outcomes, while still keeping enough hands-on fluency to know when the agent is leading them astray.

r001.rationale: The response says agent work depends on clearly specifying intent and that vague requests can produce wrong results, but it does not state that direct editing versus using an agent is faster depending on how clearly the person knows what they want.

r002.rationale: It says the joy shifts to system design and product thinking, and to seeing ambitious work come together quickly, linking agents with focusing on creating and building.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been one of the stranger transitions of my career, because the thing I was good at, and the thing I enjoyed, was the act of writing code. Sitting down, getting into flow, building the thing by hand. And that's mostly gone now. What I do instead is closer to being a tech lead for a team of very fast, very capable, slightly amnesiac junior engineers.

The first thing you notice is that your bottleneck moves. It used to be typing and thinking through implementation details. Now it's specification and verification. How clearly can I describe what I actually want? And how quickly can I tell whether what came back is right? Those were always important skills, but they were kind of secondary. Now they're the whole job.

The second thing is that your sense of the code changes. When you write every line yourself, you have this intimate map of the system in your head. You know where the bodies are buried. When agents are writing most of it, you lose some of that, and you have to be deliberate about keeping enough of a map to still make good decisions. I've found that I read a lot more code than I write now, and I read it differently, more like a reviewer than an author.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is the emotional part. There's a real sense of loss. Flow state was a big part of why I liked this work. Orchestrating is a different kind of satisfaction. It's less about craft and more about leverage. Some days that feels amazing, because I can ship in an afternoon what used to take a week. Other days I miss just building something with my own hands.

So I'd say I'm still figuring out what the craft is in this new mode. I think it exists. I think it's in the taste, in the judgment about what to build and what to throw away, and in designing the harness around the agents so they fail in ways you can catch. But it's a different craft than the one I spent twenty years learning.

r001.rationale: The response says specification becomes the bottleneck and asks how clearly the person can describe what they want, but it does not state that direct editing is faster than using an agent depending on that clarity.

r002.rationale: The response describes agent orchestration as a different kind of satisfaction, focused more on leverage, and says the speaker misses building by hand. It does not attribute joy in using agents to focusing on creating and building.

astra-6.text:
For me, the biggest shift is where you put your attention. When you’re writing code yourself, you’re constantly moving between the thing you want to build and the details of how to make it work. With agents, more of your attention goes toward defining the problem, giving enough context, and deciding whether the result actually does what you intended.

And that’s a different kind of effort. You can give an agent a vague instruction and get back something that looks very complete, but it may have resolved every ambiguity differently than you would have. So you have to get better at making your assumptions explicit—and at checking the outcome without feeling like you need to personally reconstruct every line of code.

I think the interesting tension is that you can do more in parallel, but your ability to evaluate the work becomes the bottleneck. It’s easy to start five things. It’s harder to maintain enough context to know whether all five are going in the right direction. So the skill I’m trying to develop is knowing where my attention actually changes the outcome: when to intervene, when to clarify, and when to let the agent keep working.

r001.rationale: The response says vague instructions can lead to different assumptions, but it does not compare the speed of direct editing with using an agent or say that the comparison depends on how clearly the person knows what they want.

r002.rationale: The response describes shifting attention toward defining problems and evaluating results, but it does not attribute Dan’s joy in using agents to focusing on creating and building.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the biggest shift is where the effort goes. When I’m writing code myself, I’m holding the implementation in my head and working through it line by line. With coding agents, more of the work becomes defining the problem, giving them the right context, and figuring out whether what comes back actually solves it.

And that can be a little disorienting, because producing code used to be such a tangible measure of progress. Now I might spend more time reading code than writing it. But I still need to understand the system well enough to ask good questions and catch mistakes. So it feels less like giving up engineering and more like moving up a level of abstraction—with a much greater emphasis on judgment.
